Amend phy_get(), of_phy_get() and devm_of_phy_get_by_index() to fix the same usage pattern. phy_provider_unregister() must take the phy_provider_mutex so amending phy_get()/of_phy_get() to take that same mutex guarantees there is no use-after-free.

t: power: supply: pf1550: drain IRQ work before unregistering supplies
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: power: supply: pf1550: drain IRQ work before unregistering supplies The VBUS work calls power_supply_changed(), but its managed cancellation is registered before the supplies. Cleanup can therefore unregister a supply while IRQ-triggered work is still pending. Commit 838767f50747 ("power: supply: pf1550: Fix use-after-free in power_supply_changed()") moved IRQ requests after supply registration, but left work cancellation before the supplies. That change protects the direct IRQ callbacks, while this fix drains the work they queue. Register the three work items after both supplies and before the IRQs. Cleanup then frees the IRQ producers, drains the work, and unregisters the supplies. The teardown ordering issue was found by static analysis.

t: power: supply: sbs-battery: disable polling before supply teardown
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: power: supply: sbs-battery: disable polling before supply teardown The managed poll-work cancellation is registered before the power supply, so cleanup unregisters the supply before draining polling. A pending or running poller can then call power_supply_changed() on the released supply. Commit 8d59cf3887fb ("power: supply: sbs-battery: Fix use-after-free in power_supply_changed()") moved the IRQ request after supply registration, but did not change the poll-work cancellation order. Add a later managed action that disables and drains polling before supply teardown. Its retained disabled state prevents external-power callbacks from rearming the poll work after it has been drained. Keep the original autocancel to initialize work before supply callbacks can run and to cover failed supply registration. The teardown ordering issue was found by static analysis.

t: pps: generators: don't use the driver's info after unregister
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: pps: generators: don't use the driver's info after unregister A file that was opened before pps_gen_unregister_source() keeps pps_gen, and with it the pointer to the driver's pps_gen_source_info. PPS_GEN_SETENABLE and PPS_GEN_USESYSTEMCLOCK keep using that pointer after the driver has gone: - pps_gen_tio allocates its info with devm_kzalloc(), so after an unbind both ioctls read freed memory, and SETENABLE calls the driver's enable() with its freed private data. - pps_gen-dummy does not set info->owner, so it can be unloaded while the file is open, and the ioctls then read the unloaded module's data and call its code. TIO can't probe in a VM, as it needs ART. A test driver that registers its info in devm memory like TIO does, unbound while /dev/pps-gen0 is open, gives: BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in pps_gen_cdev_ioctl+0x4c1/0x580 Read of size 1 at addr ffff88800e647f38 by task ppsgen64/145 ... Freed by task 146: kfree+0x25a/0x6d0 release_nodes+0xd1/0x140 devres_release_all+0x10e/0x1a0 device_unbind_cleanup+0x71/0x250 device_release_driver_internal+0x41b/0x570 unbind_store+0xd9/0x100 and unloading pps_gen-dummy while its file is open oopses: BUG: unable to handle page fault for address: ffffffffa0203040 Oops: Oops: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN NOPTI RIP: 0010:pps_gen_cdev_ioctl+0x372/0x580 Protect info in the ioctl handler with a mutex, and clear it under the mutex on unregister, so that unregister waits for the ioctls using it and later ones fail with -ENODEV. PPS_KC_BIND does the same for a removed PPS device since commit 3649f9a6b897 ("pps: don't allow PPS_KC_BIND on removed devices"). The sysfs attributes need nothing new: they are removed, and their callbacks drained, before info is cleared.

t: nvmem: core: Fix OOB read for bit offsets of more than one byte
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: nvmem: core: Fix OOB read for bit offsets of more than one byte When the bit offset is BITS_PER_BYTE or larger the read position is advanced by `bytes_offset`. This is not taken into account in the per-byte read loop which still reads `cell->bytes` resulting in an out of bounds read of `bytes_offset` bytes. The information read OOB does not leak directly as the erroneously read bits are cleared. Detected by KASAN while looking for a use-after-free in simplefb.c.

t: nvmet-auth: serialize access to DH-HMAC-CHAP state to fix UAF
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: nvmet-auth: serialize access to DH-HMAC-CHAP state to fix UAF A REPLY AUTH_SEND command can derive a dhchap_skey key while a concurrent AUTH_RECEIVE command observing this REPLY state executes the failure path and frees that key. The REPLY command then continues and writes into freed memory, causing a use-after-free. KASAN reports it as: BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in __sha256_final Write of size 4 at addr ffff88800359c540 ... nvmet_auth_sq_free (drivers/nvme/target/auth.c:237) nvmet_execute_auth_receive (drivers/nvme/target/fabrics-cmd-auth.c:621) Add a mutex to each submission queue to serialize authentication commands and timeout handling. Unlock the mutex before completing requests and ignore outdated timeout callbacks. Limit timeout delays to prevent immediate expiry on 32-bit kernels.

t: media: rc: Ensure that rc_unregister_device() does not free input device
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: media: rc: Ensure that rc_unregister_device() does not free input device During or after rc_unregister_device(), IR may still be reported which results in a input event being reported. This could result in a null pointer deref in rc_keydown() or a use-after-free of the input device if the pointer was read before it is set to NULL.

t: media: rc: Ensure registered is cleared in error path
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: media: rc: Ensure registered is cleared in error path If rc_register_device() fails, ensure that registered is not set to true. If lirc_register() succeeded, then userspace could have an open file descriptor open. This leads to a use-after-free. lirc_unregister() must be called with registered = false, else there is a possibility that an fd is open and polling, which would never return POLLERR unless registered is false. Note that registered must be changed under dev->lock, many functions read registered under lock (e.g. lirc_ioctl).

t: media: rc: mce_kbd: Fix inconsistent locking of keylock
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: media: rc: mce_kbd: Fix inconsistent locking of keylock data->keylock is taken with spin_lock() in ir_mce_kbd_decode(), which runs in the raw IR decode kthread with local interrupts enabled, but with spin_lock_irqsave() in mce_kbd_rx_timeout(), the rx_timeout timer callback, which runs in softirq context. If the decode kthread is holding keylock via spin_lock() when a timer interrupt fires on the same CPU and the softirq runs mce_kbd_rx_timeout(), the softirq spins forever waiting for a lock that only the now-preempted kthread can release, while the kthread cannot run again until the softirq gives up the CPU. This deadlocks the CPU.

t: media: rc: Use after free in ir_raw_event_handle()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: media: rc: Use after free in ir_raw_event_handle() If rc_unregister_device() is called while IR is being processed, then ir_raw_event_handle() could call wake_up_process(dev->raw->thread) after kthread_stop(dev->raw->thread). Avoid use after free by using get_task_struct().

t: media: rc: After rc_unregister_device() timers can be re-armed
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: media: rc: After rc_unregister_device() timers can be re-armed If rc_keydown() is called after rc_register_device(), then the timers can be re-armed. Delete them again for a final time.

t: media: rc: Fix use after free in bpf progs
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: media: rc: Fix use after free in bpf progs Since commit dccc0c3ddf8f ("media: rc: fix race between unregister and urb/irq callbacks"), rcdev->raw is no longer set to NULL after device unregister. raw->progs could point to stale data.

t: ocfs2/heartbeat: unlink live slots when their node is missing
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2/heartbeat: unlink live slots when their node is missing o2hb_shutdown_slot() returns immediately when its node is no longer in the configfs registry. A slot can still be linked in o2hb_live_slots when that lookup fails. Region teardown or startup-error cleanup then frees the slot array without removing its embedded list member. With the same peer live in another region, the next list update can follow a predecessor into the freed array. Reusing the node number can also make a later insertion encounter that stale member. Always remove the slot under o2hb_live_lock, even when node lookup fails. Preserve aggregate membership accounting and the last-region DOWN callback: the existing callback interface explicitly permits a NULL node for DOWN events. Only drop the node reference when lookup returned one. This closes both normal release and startup-abort paths without changing the publication or callback locking protocol. Also require a configured node before admitting a new live slot in o2hb_check_slot(). The early live-bitmap check is not held through admission: the last live slot in another region can be removed in between. Without a node, admission can then queue an UP event with a NULL argument and hit the event helper's BUG_ON. Existing live slots can still leave and generate NULL-node DOWN events. A controlled probe-instrumented test reproduced this while stopping one of two regions after removing the peer from configfs. t: ocfs2/dlm: hold a lock reference across grant AST enqueue
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2/dlm: hold a lock reference across grant AST enqueue A newly granted remote lock must remain alive until its grant AST is queued. dlmlock_master() publishes the lock on res->granted with its base and queue references, then drops res->spinlock before calling dlm_queue_ast(). The resource's reserved AST count does not retain the lock itself. This can fail when a peer dies with an immediately grantable CREATE buffered on its socket. O2NET's node-down callback flushes receive work before DLM cleanup, but the flush only waits for work queued on entry. A data-ready callback that already selected the socket container can queue new receive work after the flush advances its work color. Socket shutdown does not discard bytes already queued for TCP receive. The late receive work and DLM node-down cleanup can interleave as follows (the lock reference operations shown are before this fix): Socket data-ready Node-down thread Receive worker ----------------- ---------------- -------------- o2net_data_ready() select sc under callback read lock o2net_disconnect_node() queue shutdown begin flush; new color queue sc_rx_work in the new color release callback lock shutdown socket flush returns read buffered CREATE dlmlock_master() lock res->spinlock add lock to granted unlock res->spinlock DLM node-down cleanup lock res->spinlock dlm_free_dead_locks() unlink lock put queue/base refs free lock unlock res->spinlock dlm_queue_ast() __dlm_queue_ast() read lock->lockres (use-after-free) DLM cleanup holds res->spinlock while dlm_free_dead_locks() drops the queue and base references. The CREATE handler no longer holds that spinlock when __dlm_queue_ast() reads the lock, before taking its AST list reference. Take a temporary lock reference under res->spinlock when a grant AST will be queued, and drop it after dlm_queue_ast(). This keeps the lock alive across cleanup until the AST path has taken its own reference, without reversing the existing AST/resource lock order. KASAN report as below: BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in __dlm_queue_ast+0x8a4/0xc00 Read of size 8 at addr ffff88810ead5940 by task kworker/u16:3/52 CPU: 3 UID: 0 PID: 52 Comm: kworker/u16:3 Not tainted 7.3.0-rc4-next-20260921-pmb-bt-functional-v1+ #1 PREEMPT(lazy) Hardware name: QEMU Ubuntu 24.04 PC v2 (i440FX + PIIX, arch_caps fix, 1996), BIOS 1.16.3-debian-1.16.3-2 04/01/2014 Workqueue: o2net o2net_rx_until_empty Call Trace: <TASK> dump_stack_lvl+0x93/0xd0 print_report+0xce/0x630 ? __dlm_queue_ast+0x8a4/0xc00 ? srso_alias_return_thunk+0x5/0xfbef5 ? __virt_addr_valid+0x20e/0x420 ? __dlm_queue_ast+0x8a4/0xc00 kasan_report+0xe0/0x110 ? __dlm_queue_ast+0x8a4/0xc00 __dlm_queue_ast+0x8a4/0xc00 ? srso_alias_return_thunk+0x5/0xfbef5 ? srso_alias_return_thunk+0x5/0xfbef5 ? do_raw_spin_lock+0x130/0x270 ? __pfx___dlm_queue_ast+0x10/0x10 ? __pfx_do_raw_spin_lock+0x10/0x10 ? _raw_spin_unlock_irqrestore+0x45/0x60 ? srs ---truncated---

t: ocfs2/dlm: hold the lookup reference across convert AST enqueue
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2/dlm: hold the lookup reference across convert AST enqueue dlm_convert_lock_handler() drops the reference it took when it found the lock on res->granted at its leave label, one statement before it calls dlm_queue_ast(). dlm_free_dead_locks() takes res->spinlock and drops the list and base references, so a peer death landing in that gap leaves the handler's own put as the one that frees the lock, and __dlm_queue_ast() then reads lock->lockres from freed memory. The handler is registered next to dlm_create_lock_handler(), so a convert message buffered on a dying peer's socket arrives on the same o2net receive work that o2net_disconnect_node() does not wait for. The two can interleave as follows, with the reference counts as they are before this fix: Socket data-ready Node-down thread Receive worker ----------------- ---------------- -------------- o2net_data_ready() select sc under callback read lock o2net_disconnect_node() queue shutdown begin flush; new color queue sc_rx_work in the new color release callback lock shutdown socket flush returns read buffered convert_lock dlm_convert_lock_handler() find lock on res->granted dlm_lock_get() refs = 3 lock res->spinlock __dlmconvert_master() call_ast = 1 unlock res->spinlock DLM node-down cleanup lock res->spinlock dlm_free_dead_locks() unlink lock put list ref refs = 2 put base ref refs = 1 unlock res->spinlock dlm_lock_put() refs = 0 free lock dlm_queue_ast() __dlm_queue_ast() read lock->lockres (use-after-free) __dlmconvert_master() only moves the lock between lists, so the count entering the gap is base, list and lookup. Drop the lookup reference after the AST is queued instead of before it and the race ends with the one __dlm_queue_ast() took, which dlm_flush_asts() releases later with ast_pending cleared and ast_list unlinked. No extra get is needed, and the normal case ends with the same count as before. dlmconvert_master() has the same shape but is only reached from dlmlock() for a lock this node owns, which dlm_free_dead_locks() never matches.

t: ocfs2: cancel quota sync work before freeing quota info
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2: cancel quota sync work before freeing quota info OCFS2 quota info owns dqi_sync_work and must outlive both its timer and qsync_work_fn(). ocfs2_local_free_info() frees that owner without cancelling the work, relying on the quota suspend/disable wrappers. Loading quotas on a read-only to read-write remount can successfully queue the work in ocfs2_global_read_info() and then fail while attaching a dquot to an existing inode in add_dquot_ref(). The quota core unwinds that failure directly through dquot_disable(), bypassing the OCFS2 wrapper: Remount task (s_umount write) Timer/workqueue ocfs2_global_read_info() schedules dqi_sync_work add_dquot_ref() returns an error dquot_disable() ocfs2_local_free_info() frees oinfo delayed-work timer expires qsync_work_fn() reads oinfo The timer core can then write to the freed embedded timer, or qsync_work_fn() can read oinfo->dqi_gqinode before its s_umount trylock. The outer ocfs2_disable_quotas() cleanup skips the failed type because dquot_disable() has already cleared its loaded state. Cancel dqi_sync_work synchronously at the start of ocfs2_local_free_info(), before dropping the global inode or freeing any owner state. The work is initialized whenever read_file_info() succeeds. dquot_disable() holds s_umount for write, so the callback skips its quota scan via down_read_trylock() and can finish without waiting for teardown. The synchronous cancel also handles its self-rearm. t: ocfs2: fix chunk number of the first chunk in a local quota file
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2: fix chunk number of the first chunk in a local quota file Mounting a crafted OCFS2 image can corrupt kernel memory. When the local quota file header of such an image claims zero chunks, the first quota entry allocated during the mount gets a chunk number taken from a kernel pointer, and releasing that entry clears a bit far outside the chunk bitmap. The write will corrupt the data stored at that address, and the corruption may lead to a system crash or damage unrelated data. Mounting requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN, so it takes an untrusted image, such as removable media or a loop mount of a file from elsewhere. Since the chunk number comes from a kernel pointer, the address of the bit that gets cleared differs from boot to boot, and the issue has been reported under several titles: - BUG: unable to handle kernel paging request in ocfs2_local_release_dquot - KASAN: use-after-free Write in ocfs2_local_release_dquot - KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds Write in ocfs2_local_release_dquot - KASAN: slab-use-after-free Write in ocfs2_local_release_dquot - KFENCE: use-after-free write in ocfs2_local_release_dquot Note that none of these is a use-after-free in the quota code: the chunk and its buffer head are alive. The bit that gets cleared lies far outside the bitmap. KASAN and KFENCE name each report based on the object occupying that address, which explains why the same issue is reported under so many different titles. In the report I sent, the address fell in a free page, which KASAN labels use-after-free. There are known reproducers. Both a syzkaller and a C reproducer are available from the Google Drive link [1] in my report thread. The issue was found by our modified syzkaller, not a theoretical thing found by an LLM. I have not seen it outside fuzzing, so it is not affecting me in the real world. The local quota file in OCFS2 is divided into chunks, and each chunk begins with a header block holding a bitmap of the quota entries that chunk has handed out. Chunks are numbered from zero, and that number is used to convert the file offset of an entry back into a bit position in the bitmap. ocfs2_local_quota_add_chunk() appends a new chunk to the in-memory list and numbers it one past the chunk that was last: list_add_tail(&chunk->qc_chunk, &oinfo->dqi_chunk); chunk->qc_num = list_entry(chunk->qc_chunk.prev, struct ocfs2_quota_chunk, qc_chunk)->qc_num + 1; The predecessor is looked up after the new chunk is added to the list, so if the list was empty, the prev pointer is the list head itself. The head is the dqi_chunk member of struct ocfs2_mem_dqinfo and is not a chunk, so reading qc_num through it lands 16 bytes past the start of the head, on the dqi_gqinode pointer that follows it. The first chunk of the file is then numbered with the lower half of a kernel pointer instead of 0. The list is empty when the local quota file header claims the file has no chunks. ocfs2_local_read_info() takes dqi_chunks from that header without validating it, so an image with dqi_chunks == 0 takes this path when the first quota entry is allocated. ocfs2_create_local_dquot() turns the bad number into a file offset with ol_dqblk_off(), which shifts a 32-bit block number left by the block size bits, so the top bits of such a large block number are lost. ocfs2_local_release_dquot() turns the offset back into a bit index with ol_dqblk_chunk_off(), using the full chunk number, so the lost bits push that index far outside the bitmap, and clearing it corrupts unrelated memory. Compute the chunk number before putting the chunk on the list, and use 0 when the list is empty.

t: ocfs2: pin refcount trees before dropping the lookup lock
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2: pin refcount trees before dropping the lookup lock A refcount tree returned to ocfs2_lock_refcount_tree() must stay alive until that caller releases its operation reference. However, ocfs2_get_refcount_tree() returns the cached pointer after dropping osb_lock, and the caller only takes its kref afterwards. The registry reference does not protect this gap from concurrent removal. This can happen when another node frees a refcount root and reuses its block with a different generation while this mount retains the old cached tree. Two local operations on different inodes sharing the new root, such as data CoW and an external xattr update, can then look up the same stale tree. Their inode locks are independent, and both the REFCOUNT DLM lock and rf_sem are acquired after the first operation reference. The following ordering is possible, with no other operation references: Data CoW Xattr update -------- ------------ Look up the old tree under osb_lock, then drop osb_lock Look up the same tree and take a kref Acquire the tree locks and read the new on-disk generation Erase the old tree under osb_lock Unlock and drop the operation kref Drop the registry kref, freeing tree Take a kref through the freed tree pointer The final kref_get() accesses freed rf_getcnt storage, and subsequent accesses in ocfs2_lock_refcount_tree() also use the freed allocation. Take the operation reference in ocfs2_get_refcount_tree() before releasing osb_lock, including when an insertion loses to another lookup. Removal must acquire the same lock, so it cannot drop the registry reference before the lookup has pinned the tree. Keep the existing unlock and error path puts. The two callers that already hold the refcount tree lock keep their borrowed lookup behavior and do not acquire an extra reference. KASAN report as below: BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in ocfs2_lock_refcount_tree+0x94a/0x9b0 Read of size 4 at addr ffff888117212820 by task python3/497 [Kernel and hardware identification omitted.] Call Trace: <TASK> dump_stack_lvl+0x93/0xd0 print_report+0xce/0x630 ? ocfs2_lock_refcount_tree+0x94a/0x9b0 ? srso_alias_return_thunk+0x5/0xfbef5 ? __virt_addr_valid+0x20e/0x420 ? ocfs2_lock_refcount_tree+0x94a/0x9b0 kasan_report+0xe0/0x110 ? ocfs2_lock_refcount_tree+0x94a/0x9b0 ocfs2_lock_refcount_tree+0x94a/0x9b0 ? __pfx_ocfs2_lock_refcount_tree+0x10/0x10 ? srso_alias_return_thunk+0x5/0xfbef5 ? ocfs2_refcount_cow+0x3b6/0xd90 ? srso_alias_return_thunk+0x5/0xfbef5 ? __kmalloc_cache_noprof+0x28d/0x610 ? ocfs2_refcount_cow+0x3b6/0xd90 ocfs2_refcount_cow+0x410/0xd90 ? __pfx_ocfs2_refcount_cow+0x10/0x10 ? __pfx___might_resched+0x10/0x10 ? down_write+0x11a/0x1f0 ? __pfx_down_write+0x10/0x10 ? ocfs2_inode_unlock+0x1a9/0x260 ? __pfx_ocfs2_inode_unlock+0x10/0x10 ? ocfs2_file_write_iter+0x1413/0x1d30 ocfs2_file_write_iter+0x157b/0x1d30 ? __pfx_ocfs2_file_write_iter+0x10/0x10 ? lock_acquire+0x190/0x300 ? __x64_sys_pwrite64+0x1b7/0x220 ? __pfx___might_resched+0x10/0x10 ? srso_alias_return_thunk+0x5/0xfbef5 ? security_file_permission+0x26/0x80 ? srso_alias_return_thunk+0x5/0xfbef5 ? lock_is_held_type+0x8f/0x100 vfs_write+0x639/0x1010 ? __pfx_ocfs2_file_write_iter+0x10/0x10 ? lock_vma_under_rcu+0x154/0x4a0 ? __pfx_vfs_write+0x10/0x10 ? lock_release+0x121/0x290 ? srso_alias_return_thunk+0x5/0xfbef5 __x64_sys_pwrite64+0x1b7/0x220 ? __pfx___x64_sys_pwrite64+0x10/0x10 ? irqentry_exit+0xbe/0x820 ---truncated---

t: ocfs2: snapshot dentry names in file and setattr traces
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ocfs2: snapshot dentry names in file and setattr traces Patch series "ocfs2: stabilize dentry names in file and setattr traces", v4. Snapshot names at all six users of ocfs2__file_ops and at the separate setattr event. Patch 1 handles the five ordinary file-operation callers and setattr. Patch 2 handles release separately to preserve its locked open-count sample and take the snapshot outside that critical section. The release explanation distinguishes its existing RCU lifetime coverage from name/length consistency. It does not claim that the ordinary callers' external-name UAF interleaving crosses the held inode spinlock. The release source change is unchanged from v3. Patch 1 also removes the read callback's redundant NULL-inode check. The two patches apply independently and leave trace formats unchanged. This patch (of 2): The open, fsync, read, write and splice-read trace calls pass the live dentry name and length to the shared ocfs2__file_ops event class. ocfs2_setattr() passes the same unprotected arguments to its own event. Both events size and copy a __string field separately. A reference to the dentry does not pin the external storage backing an individual name. With an event enabled, a caller can be preempted after loading the name pointer. A long-to-short rename can then replace the name and reclaim its old external allocation before the trace callback sizes or copies it, provided no other snapshot retains that allocation. The setattr inode lock does not exclude every rename: a same-directory rename of a source directory need not take that directory's inode lock. It can therefore change the dentry name while setattr records its event. Inline names and separately loaded lengths can also change during trace record sizing and copying. Take a dentry name snapshot around each of these six trace calls and pass both the string and length from the snapshot. Check event enablement before taking a snapshot. Keep the event classes and formats unchanged. Also remove the redundant NULL-inode check in the read callback. file_inode() returns the open file's inode, which is already used by the trace call above the check. The historical report below is from the read path. KASAN report as below: BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in strlen+0x85/0xa0 Read of size 1 at addr ffff88810a5b2b18 by task python3/496 [CPU and host details omitted.] Call Trace: <TASK> dump_stack_lvl+0x93/0xd0 print_report+0xce/0x630 ? strlen+0x85/0xa0 ? srso_alias_return_thunk+0x5/0xfbef5 ? __virt_addr_valid+0x20e/0x420 ? strlen+0x85/0xa0 kasan_report+0xe0/0x110 ? strlen+0x85/0xa0 strlen+0x85/0xa0 trace_event_raw_event_ocfs2__file_ops+0xf0/0x480 ? __pfx_trace_event_raw_event_ocfs2__file_ops+0x10/0x10 ? srso_alias_return_thunk+0x5/0xfbef5 ? pmbd_probe_hit_cookie+0xe7/0x1c0 ? srso_alias_return_thunk+0x5/0xfbef5 ? __pfx_pmbd_probe_hit_cookie+0x10/0x10 ocfs2_file_read_iter+0x6cd/0xb30 ? __pfx_ocfs2_file_read_iter+0x10/0x10 ? selinux_file_permission+0x11d/0x540 ? srso_alias_return_thunk+0x5/0xfbef5 ? security_file_permission+0x26/0x80 vfs_read+0x7d2/0xc20 ? __pfx_vfs_read+0x10/0x10 ? srso_alias_return_thunk+0x5/0xfbef5 ? __pfx_do_sys_openat2+0x10/0x10 ksys_read+0x111/0x200 ? __pfx_ksys_read+0x10/0x10 ? irqentry_exit+0xbe/0x820 ? srso_alias_return_thunk+0x5/0xfbef5 ? trace_hardirqs_on_prepare+0x11d/0x150 ? srso_alias_return_thunk+0x5/0xfbef5 do_syscall_64+0x114/0x620 entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x77/0x7f [User register dump omitted.] </TASK> Allocated by task 489: kasan_save_stack+0x33/0x60 kasan_save_track+0x14/0x30 __kasan_kmalloc+0xaa/0xb0 __kmalloc_noprof+0x2de/0x780 __d_alloc+0x5fc/0x8c0 d_alloc_parallel+0x106/0x11d0 lookup_open+0x3ff/0 ---truncated---

t: smb: client: fix OOB last_entry pointer from unbounded LastNameOffset
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: smb: client: fix OOB last_entry pointer from unbounded LastNameOffset CIFSFindFirst() and CIFSFindNext() locate the last entry of a TRANS2_FIND_FIRST2 or TRANS2_FIND_NEXT2 response by adding the LastNameOffset of the response parameters to the start of the data area, and store the result in psrch_inf->last_entry. MS-CIFS 2.2.6.2.2 defines that offset as the offset of the entry's file name; the client follows the reading of NT and Samba servers, which point it at the entry. LastNameOffset is only checked against CIFSMaxBufSize, which says nothing about the response actually received: validate_t2() lets the data area start up to 1024 bytes into the buffer, and SendReceive() copies at most CIFSMaxBufSize + MAX_CIFS_HDR_SIZE bytes of a response, 16468 by default, into a cifs_request allocation of CIFSMaxBufSize + MAX_SMB2_HDR_SIZE bytes, 16588 by default. The pointer itself can therefore be placed anywhere from the end of the received data to 820 bytes past the end of the allocation. The read through that pointer is far larger than its displacement. find_cifs_entry() hands last_entry to cifs_save_resume_key() after every FindNext and after the FindFirst of a search rewind, and cifs_fill_dirent() takes the length of the name from the entry itself: a __le32 FileNameLength for most levels, a __u8 for SMB_FIND_FILE_INFO_STANDARD, and for SMB_FIND_FILE_UNIX the result of a scan for the terminating NUL over up to PATH_MAX + 1 UTF-16 units. The name is recorded as the resume name of the search, and the next CIFSFindNext() rejects only a recorded length of PATH_MAX or more before copying the name into the ResumeFileName of its request and sending it with the resume key taken from the same entry: up to 4 KiB of memory from past the end of the allocation leaks to the server, and for SMB_FIND_FILE_UNIX the NUL scan runs about twice as far before the length is even known. The entry does not have to lie outside the response for that either: a maximal response ends about 120 bytes before the end of the allocation, so an entry in its last bytes with a name just under PATH_MAX has nearly all of that name copied from past the allocation. It needs nothing unusual from the client: a FindNext response that reports no entries and does not end the search makes find_cifs_entry() send the next FindNext at once, carrying whatever was parsed at LastNameOffset, and a search rewind can do the same after its FindFirst. SMB1 is not negotiated by default: this takes a malicious or compromised server, a mount of it with an explicit vers=1.0, which CONFIG_CIFS_ALLOW_INSECURE_LEGACY (default y) permits, and a directory listing on that mount. With KASAN enabled, a response that places the last entry past the buffer, with a large DataOffset and a LastNameOffset near the end of its range, gives: ================================================================== BUG: KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds in cifs_save_resume_key.isra.0+0x7aa/0x7f0 Read of size 4 at addr ffff88807b55c33b by task ls/83 CPU: 1 UID: 0 PID: 83 Comm: ls Not tainted 7.3.0-rc4-00457-gf14572c203d5 #69 PREEMPT(lazy) Call Trace: <TASK> kasan_report+0xdf/0x1a0 cifs_save_resume_key.isra.0+0x7aa/0x7f0 cifs_readdir+0x1ed6/0x29c0 iterate_dir+0x1c0/0x570 __x64_sys_getdents64+0x133/0x270 do_syscall_64+0x109/0x5d0 entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x77/0x7f </TASK> Allocated by task 83 on cpu 0 at 19.317556s: cifs_buf_get+0x36/0x90 smb_init+0x4f/0x110 CIFSFindNext+0xf7/0x14c0 cifs_readdir+0xf51/0x29c0 The buggy address belongs to the object at ffff88807b558000 which belongs to the cache cifs_request of size 16588 The buggy address is located 623 bytes to the right of allocated 16588-byte region [ffff88807b558000, ffff88807b55c0cc) ================================================================== The four bytes read there are the FileNameLength of the entry, which cifs_fill_dirent() tak ---truncated---

t: smb: client: hold server info until cifsd exits
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: smb: client: hold server info until cifsd exits The last session reference can be dropped while the cifsd demultiplex thread is still running clean_demultiplex_info(). That thread frees TCP_Server_Info there, racing with cifs_put_tcp_session() as it releases the server crypto state. syzbot reported a KASAN use-after-free in cifs_crypto_secmech_release(). Keep an object reference for the cifsd thread. Defer final crypto, session-key, network namespace, string, and structure cleanup until both the last session reference and the thread reference are dropped. Drop the thread reference after clean_demultiplex_info() has finished using the server. Build-tested with ARCH=arm64 and W=1 for fs/smb/client/connect.o. The KASAN reproducer was not run on the patched kernel.

t: ovl: hold a reference on the parent in readdir
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ovl: hold a reference on the parent in readdir Listing a directory on an overlay uses a freed dentry and crashes the kernel when a lookup moves the directory at the same time. Code that can sleep may only use d_parent without a reference while something stops a move of the dentry. ovl_iterate_real(), ovl_need_adjust_d_ino() and ovl_cache_update() use the d_parent of the listed directory and hold only the lock of that directory. When a lookup finds the directory under another parent after a change to a layer, d_splice_alias() moves it without that lock and drops its reference on the old parent. With a delay in ovl_iterate_real(), getdents64 on an overlay directory raced a rename in the lower layer and a lookup that moved its dentry, and after an rmdir of the old parent KASAN reported a use-after-free in security_inode_getattr(). Fix this by using dget_parent() in the three functions. [amir: fix comments in ovl_need_adjust_d_ino()]

t: ovl: set OVL_WHITEOUTS before publishing the upper dir
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ovl: set OVL_WHITEOUTS before publishing the upper dir Listing a directory while it is copied up causes a use-after-free of the readdir cache. A merge directory must never be iterated as a real upper directory: that mode frees the cache in OVL_I(inode)->cache without looking at its refcount, while files opened in merged mode still use it. ovl_copy_up_workdir() publishes the upper dentry before it sets OVL_WHITEOUTS, and ovl_dir_open() samples both without a lock, so an open between the two stores finds the upper directory and takes it for a real one. With a delay between the two stores, an unprivileged process that listed a directory during its copy-up saw only "." and "..", and its next getdents freed the readdir cache of another descriptor. Fix this by setting OVL_WHITEOUTS before ovl_inode_update(), so that ovl_dir_reset() agrees with ovl_dir_open(), and by testing OVL_TYPE_MERGE() of the path type in ovl_dir_open(), so that an open that observes the upper dentry never iterates a merge dir as a real dir, regardless of the order in which it observes the flag. [amir: test OVL_TYPE_MERGE() instead of smp_rmb() in ovl_dir_open()]

t: ovl: take a snapshot of the name for copy up
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ovl: take a snapshot of the name for copy up The copy up of a directory reads a freed dentry name when a lookup moves the directory at the same time. A pointer to the name of a dentry is only valid while something stops a move of the dentry. ovl_do_copy_up() keeps a plain copy of c->dentry->d_name in c->destname, and ovl_copy_up_start() only keeps ovl_rename() away. When a lookup finds the same directory under another name after a change to the lower layer, d_splice_alias() moves the dentry and frees its external name. With a delay in ovl_do_copy_up(), a chmod of a lower-only directory with a 60 byte name raced with a rename of that directory in the lower layer and a stat of the new name, and KASAN reported a use-after-free in lookup_noperm_common(). Fix this by using take_dentry_name_snapshot() for c->destname.

t: ovl: use the pinned upper dir in ovl_fix_origin()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ovl: use the pinned upper dir in ovl_fix_origin() Renames made directly on the upper filesystem during a lookup crash the kernel. A dentry that is passed to vfs_setxattr() must be pinned. ovl_fix_origin() passes upper->d_parent to ovl_set_impure() without a reference, and the lookup holds no lock of the upper directory. A rename on the upper filesystem changes d_parent, and only the child pins the new parent, so a second rename and an rmdir free it. With delays in ovl_fix_origin() and ovl_set_impure(), renaming the upper directory twice and removing the intermediate parent during the lookup of a merge directory without an origin xattr gave a KASAN use-after-free in vfs_setxattr(). Fix this by passing the upper dentry that the overlay parent holds. [amir: add helper ovl_set_impure_dir()]

t: ovl: always encode the origin fh when index is enabled
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ovl: always encode the origin fh when index is enabled On an overlay with index=on,nfs_export=on, copy up of a directory crashes the kernel once an LSM has started to deny CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH to the mounter, the task that mounted the overlay. The mount and the LSM policy change require root. After that, any user who can write to a directory that exists only in a lower layer triggers the oops by doing so. Before a file or directory that exists only in a lower layer is changed for the first time, overlayfs copies it to the writable upper layer. This is called copy up. On copy up, ovl_get_origin_fh() encodes the file handle of the lower inode, called the origin. It returns NULL if ovl_can_decode_fh() says that the lower filesystem cannot decode handles. Whether the callers can handle NULL depends on the index option: - Without an index, NULL is fine: the callers store an empty origin xattr. - With index enabled, overlayfs keeps entries for copied up inodes in an internal index directory. The name of an index entry is derived from the handle, so ovl_get_origin_fh() must return a handle or an error. The mount only enables the index if ovl_can_decode_fh() succeeds for all layers, but the result can change later. The function checks the export operations of the filesystem and capable(CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH). Copy up runs with the mounter's credentials, and an LSM can start to deny the capability to those credentials after the mount. ovl_get_origin_fh() then returns NULL with index enabled. This goes wrong in two callers: - With nfs_export=on, copy up of a directory creates an index entry for the directory. ovl_create_index() passes the NULL handle to ovl_get_index_name_fh(), which dereferences it. - If the result changes while mount(2) is still running, ovl_get_indexdir() passes a NULL from ovl_get_origin_fh() to ovl_verify_set_fh() in the same way. Before the commit in the Fixes tag, these two callers encoded the handle themselves, without consulting ovl_can_decode_fh(). Reproduced with a BPF LSM program that started to deny the capability after the mount. An unprivileged touch in a directory that had not been copied up yet oopsed in ovl_get_index_name_fh(). With this patch the touch succeeds and the directory gets its index entry. Fix this by calling ovl_can_decode_fh() in ovl_get_origin_fh() only when index is disabled.

t: ovl: check that the parents of volatile/dirty are dirs
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ovl: check that the parents of volatile/dirty are dirs An unprivileged user crashes the kernel by mounting overlayfs with the volatile option. A dentry that serves as the parent of a lookup must be a directory. ovl_create_volatile_dirty() walks work/incompat/volatile/dirty by name, and ovl_lookup_or_create() returns an existing entry whatever its type. A file or a symlink that another task creates during the mount becomes the parent of the next lookup, which calls a NULL ->lookup. An unprivileged user mounted overlayfs with "volatile" in a user namespace while a second process created a symlink named work/incompat, and the mount task oopsed on a NULL ->lookup call. Fix this by returning -ENOTDIR from ovl_lookup_or_create() when the caller asked for a directory and the existing entry is a non-dir.

t: ovl: do not copy up a dentry that was removed
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ovl: do not copy up a dentry that was removed A change to a removed file through an open descriptor replaces whatever has its old name in the upper layer. Copy up must only create a name in the upper directory, never replace one. After an unlink, an rmdir or a rename over a lower dentry, a dentry that an open file keeps alive still has its old parent and name, but in the upper directory that name is now a whiteout or a new object. ovl_copy_up_workdir() renames the copy over it, which brings back the removed object and destroys whatever took its name. An unprivileged user opened a lower FIFO and unlinked it, root created a file at that name, and fchmod on the old descriptor replaced the file of root with the FIFO. Fix this by looking up the target name of the rename in ovl_copy_up_workdir() with LOOKUP_EXCL, so that copy up fails with -EEXIST if the name is taken, as copy up with O_TMPFILE already does when it links the copy to the name. [amir: use LOOKUP_EXCL instead of relying on d_unhashed()]

t: ovl: do not copy up an xattr value that was never read
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ovl: do not copy up an xattr value that was never read Copy-up stores uninitialized kernel memory in an xattr of the upper file, where the user can read it. ovl_copy_xattr() may only pass bytes to ovl_do_setxattr() that ovl_do_getxattr() has read. When the read fails with -ERANGE the function asks for the size again, and if the new size fits the buffer it stores the buffer although nothing was read into it. The buffer comes from kvmalloc(), or it still holds the value of the previous xattr. A FUSE lower layer that answers every sized GETXATTR with -ERANGE made copy-up store 4096 bytes that the server never sent, with a kernel pointer in them, as an xattr of the upper file. Fix this by failing the copy-up with -EIO when the size that follows -ERANGE fits the buffer.

t: ovl: fix a torn path in ovl_get_redirect()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ovl: fix a torn path in ovl_get_redirect() A hard link of a metacopy file that races with a rename of an ancestor stores a redirect to the wrong lower file. Each component of an absolute redirect must be the name that a dentry has in the parent that the walk continues with. ovl_get_redirect() copies the name under d_lock and calls dget_parent() after the unlock, and the callers for a hard link hold no lock that stops a rename across directories. A rename between the two steps combines the old name with the new parent. With delays in ovl_get_redirect(), an unprivileged user hard-linked a metacopy file while renaming its ancestor to another directory, the stored redirect named another lower path, and after a remount the file showed the data of a root-only file. Fix this by taking the parent first and checking it again under d_lock.

t: ovl: read the nlink xattr of every indexed non-dir
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ovl: read the nlink xattr of every indexed non-dir With nfs_export=on, data written through a file handle to a lower file, i.e. a file that exists only in a lower layer of the overlay, can be lost on the next mount. A lookup of the file by name then returns -EIO. Also, a file with one name reports st_nlink 2 once it has been copied to the upper layer. After such a file is removed, its file handle can still open it until the next mount. Before a lower file is changed for the first time, overlayfs copies it to the writable upper layer. This is called copy up. The index directory is $workdir/index, where $workdir is the directory given by the workdir= option. Each entry is named after the file handle of a lower inode, so that overlayfs can get from the handle to the copied up inode. With nfs_export=on, copy up indexes every non-directory: it copies the file to an entry in the index directory and then hard links that entry into the upper directory. The index entry is an extra link to the upper inode, so overlayfs stores the link count that users should see in the overlay.nlink xattr. A file can also be opened by handle, either by an NFS client or by a process with CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH calling open_by_handle_at(). If the file is not in the dcache, its overlay dentry is disconnected, i.e. it has no parent yet. Copy up then creates the index entry but no hard link in the upper directory. The index entry has i_nlink 1 and holds the only copy of the data written to the file. ovl_get_nlink() reads the stored count. Its caller passes a default, which the function returns if there is no stored count. If the lower inode has i_nlink 1, the function returns the default without reading the xattr. That was correct as long as only lower files with multiple links were indexed. On the next mount, ovl_verify_index() looks for orphans, i.e. index entries of files whose last name was removed. For an index entry with i_nlink 1, it passes a default of 0 to ovl_get_nlink() and treats a result of 0 as an orphan. Here the lower inode also has i_nlink 1, so the result is the default. ovl_indexdir_cleanup() then replaces the entry with a whiteout, which in the index marks a file as deleted. The written data is lost. A lookup by name then returns -EIO, because a whiteout as the index entry of a lower file that still exists is a bad index. ovl_get_inode() gets the wrong count the same way. Its default is the i_nlink of the upper inode, which includes the index entry, so a copied up file with one name reports st_nlink 2. When that name is removed, the count drops to 1 rather than 0. ovl_nlink_end() replaces the index entry with a whiteout only at a count of 0, so the entry stays, and the handle of the removed file still opens it. Reproduced by writing through open_by_handle_at() to an uncached lower file with one link. After a remount the data was lost, and the name returned EIO. Fix this by adding an argument to ovl_get_nlink() that says whether the caller found an index entry, and by skipping the xattr only if the caller found none. Known gaps: - An index entry that a kernel without this patch left behind for a removed file now stays, and the handle of that file keeps working. The entry has i_nlink 1 and a stored count of 1, just like the entry of a file that was only written by handle. Without this patch, the next mount treated it as an orphan.

t: ovl: set the revalidate flags after d_instantiate()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ovl: set the revalidate flags after d_instantiate() stat() of a file on an overlayfs mount triggers a kernel warning and fails with ECHILD if another task is creating that file at the same time. This happens on an overlay with a FUSE upper layer, which is the layer where overlayfs creates new files. Write access to a directory on such an overlay is all a user needs to run the two tasks. The revalidate flags are DCACHE_OP_REVALIDATE and DCACHE_OP_WEAK_REVALIDATE. They tell path walk to call ->d_revalidate() or ->d_weak_revalidate() on a dentry, so that the filesystem can check that the cached dentry is still valid. An overlay dentry only has one of these flags if a dentry in one of its layers has it. FUSE dentries have the first one. When a flag is set on an overlay dentry, path walk calls ovl_dentry_revalidate_common(). That function only expects a dentry without an inode in RCU walk, while the dentry is being destroyed. For such a dentry outside of RCU walk, it hits a WARN_ON() and returns -ECHILD. So a negative overlay dentry must never have the flags set. ovl_instantiate() breaks this rule. When a task creates a file, the overlay dentry for the new name is hashed but still negative. ovl_instantiate() then works in this order: - It copies the flags from the new upper dentry to the overlay dentry. - It calls ovl_get_inode(), which can sleep in a getxattr request to the FUSE server. - Only then does it call d_instantiate(). A second task that looks up the name between the first step and the last finds a negative dentry with the flags set and revalidates it. Reproduced with a FUSE server that delays its getxattr reply: stat() of a name that was being created hit the WARN_ON() and failed with ECHILD. Fix this by setting the flags after d_instantiate().

t: ovl: skip copy up of empty security.capability
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ovl: skip copy up of empty security.capability ovl_copy_xattr() gives up if it can't read an attribute that listxattr() has named. An empty security.capability, which anybody has been able to store on any file for a long time, is such a case: it is listed, and getxattr() has nothing to return for it. A file in a lower layer that carries one can't be copied up: it can't be written to, renamed or have its mode changed. There is nothing to copy if there are no data. Go on with the next one. [amir: treat -EINVAL as no capability too, and do the same in ovl_copy_up_meta_inode_data()]

t: xfs: fix buffer overruns in xfs_ioc_attr_list
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: fix buffer overruns in xfs_ioc_attr_list When we converted the al_offset array in struct xfs_attrlist into a VLA, the size of the object shrank by 4 bytes. Unfortunately, the buffer size validation in the attrlist ioctl wasn't updated to notice this, so the al_offset[0] assignment blindly writes off the end of the buffer. LOLLM noticed the omitted check and complained.

t: xfs: avoid cross-rtgroup reaping after a repair
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: avoid cross-rtgroup reaping after a repair LOLLM notices that the extents stored in a xrtb_bitmap (aka xfs_rtblock bitmap) can span multiple rtgroups due to two circumstances. The first is that the size of an rtgroup is an exact power of two, which means that rtgroups are adjacent in the segmented xfs_rtblock_t address space. This is fairly common to reduce the amount of multiplication and division needed to handle space on the rt volume. The second is that (unlike in the original rtgroups design), rtgroups do not have fixed-location metadata like AGs do, which means that there's nothing to force a break between rtgroups. Therefore, we must loop through the rtgroups in xreap_rtmeta_extent to avoid running off the end of an rtgroup while reaping.

t: xfs: actually lock the metafile reservation when adjusting after repair
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: actually lock the metafile reservation when adjusting after repair LOLLM reported that xrep_reset_metafile_resv performs unlocked loads and stores to the metadata file space reservation counters and thus can race with other threads. Fix this by taking the lock.

t: xfs: always reset incore attr fork buffer when resetting fork
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: always reset incore attr fork buffer when resetting fork LOLLM noticed that the local format attr fork verifier depends on if_bytes being set correctly. However, the fork reset function doesn't reset that correctly, which can cause post-repair verifier failures. Fix that.

t: xfs: don't fix the directory tree if live update fails
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: don't fix the directory tree if live update fails LOLLM complains that we don't double-check dl->aborted one last time to before committing repairs to the filesystem. This is important because the live update handler could have set ->aborted if it encountered a runtime error.

t: xfs: don't proceed with xattr repair if the live update fails
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: don't proceed with xattr repair if the live update fails LOLLM observes that we ought to make one last check for failed live updates before replacing the xattr structure. Let's be cautious here.

t: xfs: don't repair fs summary counters with garbage
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: don't repair fs summary counters with garbage LOLLM noticed that if we scan the filesystem and come up with totally garbage numbers for the summary counters, we don't actually mark the scan incomplete. Because we don't do this, repair can install the garbage values into the filesystem, making things worse. Don't do that.

t: Eclipse Ditto policy enforcers ignore revokes in multi-permission and partial permission checks
d: In Eclipse Ditto versions before 3.8.15 and 3.9.0 to 3.9.8, the policy enforcers do not let a revoke win over a grant in two kinds of permission checks. Checks of several permissions at once compare the highest grant weight with the highest revoke weight across all requested permissions instead of per permission, so the "check permissions" API (`POST /api/2/checkPermissions`, available since 3.7.0) can report a set of permissions as granted although one of them is revoked. Partial permission checks, which authorize retrieving Things and Policies and determine the receivers of events, count a grant on a sub-resource although the same permission is revoked on that sub-resource for another subject of the same authorization context (or, with the memory-optimized policy evaluator, for the same subject). A requester can thereby learn about the existence of Things and Policies and receive metadata without any readable content, and an application relying on the check permissions result may grant access the policy denies. The content of retrieved Things and Policies is still filtered correctly, and modifications are not affected.

In Eclipse Ditto versions 2.0.0 to 3.8.14 and 3.9.0 to 3.9.8, the authorization check for JSON merge patch commands on Things (HTTP `PATCH` / Ditto Protocol `merge`) does not check permissions for fields deleted or set to an empty object by the patch: fields with a `null` value or an empty object value (`{}`) are skipped by the check, and Ditto's regex-based key deletion with the documented `{{ ~<regex>~ }}` syntax is not recognized as a deletion. An authenticated user with WRITE permission on any part of a Thing can therefore delete other attributes, features and the definition of that Thing, or overwrite or create fields as empty objects, including parts the policy revokes or never grants WRITE on. -->

t: Eclipse Ditto resolved policy view discloses non-readable content of imported, namespace root and referenced policy entries
d: In Eclipse Ditto versions 3.9.0 to 3.9.8, the resolved policy view (`GET /api/2/policies/{policyId}?policy-view=resolved`) does not restrict merged policy content to what the caller may read in the policy it originates from. Imported and namespace-root entries are returned in full as soon as the caller may read any part of them in the source policy, entries of transitive imports and of the imports of namespace-root policies are only checked against the intermediate policy, and content copied into an entry by `references`, also from another entry of the same policy, is not checked against the referenced entry. An authenticated caller with READ on a policy can therefore read subjects, resources and granted/revoked permissions of policy entries that are hidden from them, including by explicit revokes, when reading the originating policy directly.

t: MISP Protected Event Signature Bypass via Whitespace Injection in JSON Keys and Identifiers
d: MISP contains a vulnerability in the cryptographic signature verification of protected events. When a MISP instance signs a protected event for synchronization, it strips all whitespace from the JSON body before computing the PGP signature (preg_replace("/\s+/", "", $data)). The receiving instance performs the same whitespace-stripping before verification. Because the signature covers only the whitespace-free representation, a network relay positioned between two MISP instances can insert whitespace characters into JSON object keys (effectively renaming fields) or into identifier values such as UUIDs, timestamps, and distribution fields without invalidating the signature. The receiving instance accepts the modified event as authentic. The vulnerability affects the protected event synchronization path: event creation (EventsController::add), event editing (EventsController::edit), event viewing (EventsController::view1), and server-to-server pull synchronization (ServerSyncTool, Server model). An attacker with a network position to intercept and modify traffic between MISP instances can alter the semantic content of protected events while the PGP signature still validates, undermining the integrity guarantees that protected events are designed to provide. The fix introduces two complementary mechanisms. First, a post-verification scan rejects any received body that contains whitespace in JSON keys (except under Galaxy cluster 'meta' keys) or in identifier-like values (uuid, id, timestamp, distribution, date). Second, a new exact-byte signature scheme (x-pgp-signature-v2) signs the body as transmitted, without whitespace normalization. MISP 3.0 and later peers exchange this exact-byte signature; older peers retain the legacy whitespace-stripped signature. A signature_version field is embedded in protected events so that a 3.0 receiver refuses a body carrying that marker if only the legacy signature is present. Both mechanisms together close the whitespace-injection vector while preserving backward compatibility with pre-3.0 instances.

In Eclipse Ditto versions 2.4.0 to 3.9.8, Thing fields a requester is not allowed to read can be disclosed through the `condition` and `live-channel-condition` headers, which are evaluated against the full Thing: the READ check of `live-channel-condition` is skipped when a `condition` header is also present on Thing query commands (3.0.0 to 3.9.8); both headers are evaluated without any authorization on WoT Thing Description requests (`Accept: application/td+json`) when WoT TD permission filtering is not active (by default in 3.0.0 to 3.8.14, in 2.4.x with WoT integration enabled, and in 3.9.x with filtering disabled); the `condition` of live messages and live events is evaluated without a READ check, and of claim messages without any permission (3.1.0 to 3.9.8); and the twin response of a Thing query with a non-matching `live-channel-condition` is returned without filtering it by the policy (3.0.0 to 3.9.8). This allows an authenticated user to read Thing fields they are not allowed to read, in some cases without any permission on the Thing.

t: Elazarl goproxy before 1.9.4 Predictable MITM Leaf Certificate Private Keys
d: Goproxy before 1.9.4 contains a weak key generation vulnerability in NewCounterEncryptorRandFromKey that derives RSA and Ed25519 leaf certificate private keys from public data due to misuse of hash.Sum. Attackers with the CA certificate and one observed leaf certificate can regenerate that host's leaf private key and impersonate the host to clients trusting the proxy CA.

In Eclipse Ditto versions before 3.9.9, Thing events delivered via WebSocket, Server-Sent Events and connections disclose field values which the policy does not allow the subscriber to read. A READ revoke for one subject of the subscriber's authorization context is not applied when another of its subjects is granted READ. For subscribers with partial READ access, subscription RQL filters, the SSE `_context`, `thing-json` placeholders and extra fields are evaluated on the unfiltered event. This allows an authenticated subscriber with at least partial READ access to a Thing to obtain the values of fields it may not read when events for that Thing are emitted.

t: xfs: fix lost errno returned from xfarray_foliosort
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: fix lost errno returned from xfarray_foliosort LOLLM noticed that we stop the sort early but don't actually pass along the error code, which could enable repair code to continue running with an unsorted array. Fix that.

t: xfs: abort dirtree repair if the live update hook dies
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: abort dirtree repair if the live update hook dies LOLLM notices that if the live update hook for the directory tree repair code hits an error, it will set dl->aborted and stops working. If the repair code ever sees that condition, it ought to bail out immediately instead of continuing with obsolete data.

t: xfs: check fork type against dabtree block magic number
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: check fork type against dabtree block magic number LOLLM complains that we fail to flag dabtree blocks that should never be associated with the file fork -- data forks can't point to xattr leaves, and attr forks can't point to dirent blocks. Add the missing checks.

t: xfs: mark overfull dabtree node blocks as corrupt
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: mark overfull dabtree node blocks as corrupt LOLLM observes that we need to range-check the dabtree node record count before using it to index an array. Fix that.

t: netfilter: nft_payload: restrict checksum offsets to known values
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: netfilter: nft_payload: restrict checksum offsets to known values We need to prevent userspace from corrupting e.g. tcp->doff, because many locations in conntrack and conntrack helpers rely on nf_conntrack_in() having validated the packet headers. nft_payload allows to alter headers later which invalidates this assumption. The 'Fixes' commit restricts writes to safe fields, but there is another side channel: the checksum location. Restrict this too. Reported via sashiko/gemini.

t: rtnetlink: wait for RCU readers in rtnl_link_unregister()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: rtnetlink: wait for RCU readers in rtnl_link_unregister() rtnl_link_ops_get() finds ops on link_ops under rcu_read_lock() and only then takes ops->srcu. rtnl_link_unregister() unlinks ops, then calls synchronize_srcu() and cleanup_srcu_struct() without first waiting for RCU readers. A reader that found ops before list_del_rcu() and has not yet taken ops->srcu is not waited for. Such a reader then locks a cleaned-up srcu_struct and keeps using ops after the module that owns it is gone. rtnl_newlink() and rtnl_dump_ifinfo() both look up ops without RTNL, the latter for any user that dumps links filtered by kind. With delays added between the lookup and srcu_read_lock() in rtnl_link_ops_get(), and before rtnl_link_ops_put() in rtnl_dump_ifinfo(), running "ip link show type dummy" alongside "rmmod dummy" on a KASAN kernel gives: BUG: KASAN: vmalloc-out-of-bounds in __srcu_read_unlock+0x57/0x70 Read of size 8 at addr ffffffffc02ff318 by task ip/147 Call Trace: __srcu_read_unlock+0x57/0x70 rtnl_dump_ifinfo.cold+0x30/0x3b rtnl_dumpit+0x7a/0x1b0 netlink_dump+0x486/0x11b0 __netlink_dump_start+0x661/0x910 rtnetlink_rcv_msg+0x611/0x9e0 netlink_rcv_skb+0x126/0x380 netlink_unicast+0x605/0x830 netlink_sendmsg+0x6d0/0xbb0 __sys_sendto+0x335/0x3a0 Call synchronize_rcu() before synchronize_srcu(), as rtnl_af_unregister() already does. This should be enough because rtnl_link_ops_get() is the only RCU walker of link_ops, and it takes ops->srcu before rcu_read_unlock(), so every reader that found ops is covered by synchronize_srcu() once the RCU grace period ends. The extra grace period only costs time at module unload. Readers and the writer were serialized by RTNL until link_ops got its own mutex, which is why the missing RCU wait did not matter before.

t: xfs: reject out-of-range attribute value lengths in xfs_attr_copy_value
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: reject out-of-range attribute value lengths in xfs_attr_copy_value xfs_attr_copy_value() takes the value length as a signed int and, for a remote xattr, is handed args->rmtvaluelen. That field is filled from the on-disk __be32 xfs_attr_leaf_name_remote.valuelen in xfs_attr3_leaf_getvalue(), so a crafted length such as 0x80000000 is stored into the signed rmtvaluelen as a negative number. The "buffer too small" guard in xfs_attr_copy_value() is a signed comparison: if (args->valuelen < valuelen) return -ERANGE; A negative valuelen therefore compares as smaller than the caller's buffer size, skips the -ERANGE path, and is then used as a copy length, leading to an out-of-bounds copy of a full remote block into a small getxattr(2) buffer on a mounted crafted image. Reject a value length that is negative or larger than the maximum xattr size before it is used, so a bogus on-disk length can no longer slip through the value copier.

t: xfs: reject remote xattr entries with an out-of-range value length
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: reject remote xattr entries with an out-of-range value length xfs_attr3_leaf_verify_entry() validates a remote attribute entry's name but never bounds its on-disk value length (xfs_attr_leaf_name_remote. valuelen, a __be32). A crafted leaf with valuelen = 0x80000000 passes the verifier and the CRC. That length is later assigned into the signed int args->rmtvaluelen (xfs_attr3_leaf_getvalue), becoming negative, which slips past the signed -ERANGE check in xfs_attr_copy_value(); a getxattr() with a small buffer then memcpy()s a full remote block into the small kvalue buffer (xfs_attr_rmtval_copyout) -- a heap out-of-bounds write with attacker-controlled content, from an unprivileged getxattr(2) on a mounted crafted image. Reject remote entries whose value length exceeds XFS_XATTR_SIZE_MAX in the leaf verifier, so the malicious block is rejected at read time.

t: MISP Push Mechanism Discloses Unpublished and Inaccessible Events to Remote Server
d: MISP contains an authorization and input-validation flaw in its event push mechanism. When a user with push permissions initiates a push of events to a remote MISP instance, the system fails to enforce two critical checks: (1) it does not verify that an event is published before including it in the push, allowing unpublished (i.e., not yet publicly shared) events to be transmitted to the remote server; and (2) it does not verify that the pushing user has read access to the event, causing events the user cannot fetch to be sent as empty event shells, thereby disclosing the existence and metadata of events the user is not authorized to view. Additionally, the remote server's reply selecting which offered events to accept is used without validating that the selected identifiers actually correspond to events in the offered set, potentially allowing the remote to reference events outside the intended scope. The vulnerability requires an authenticated user with push permissions on the source MISP instance and a configured push target. The security impact is unauthorized disclosure of confidential threat-intelligence data (unpublished events and events restricted by user permissions) to a remote MISP instance that should not receive them.

t: xfs: always forget cached ACLs if the attr fork swap succeeds
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: always forget cached ACLs if the attr fork swap succeeds LOLLM complains that xrep_xattr_rebuild_tree omits the xfs_forget_acl call if the attr fork swap succeeds (and hence the acls might have changed) but reaping the old attr fork fails. Fix it so that we always purge the cached acls if the swap succeeds, even if subsequent steps do not. This avoids some cache coherency problems with access controls.

t: xfs: always report inode repair setup failures
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: always report inode repair setup failures LOLLM noticed that xchk_setup_inode silently discards errors being returned by xrep_setup_inode. Fix that, and fix the stub macro so that it actually "returns" a value.

t: xfs: bound da-node entry count against the correct geometry
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: bound da-node entry count against the correct geometry xfs_da3_node_verify() bounds the node entry count against the larger of the directory and attribute geometries because, as a buffer verifier, it cannot tell whether the block belongs to the directory or the attribute tree. When the directory block size exceeds the fs block size (e.g. mkfs.xfs -n size=64k -b size=4k), an attribute node buffer is a single fs block that holds only m_attr_geo->node_ents entries, yet a crafted attr node may claim a count up to m_dir_geo->node_ents and still pass the verifier. xfs_da3_node_lookup_int() then indexes btree[] up to that count during its binary search -- an out-of-bounds read via getxattr/listxattr on a mounted crafted image. The buffer verifier is the wrong place to tighten this: it has no fork context, and the transaction-less read path used by getxattr does not run xfs_da3_node_set_type() either. xfs_da3_node_lookup_int(), on the other hand, always runs on that path and holds args->geo, the geometry of the fork actually being searched. Bound the entry count against args->geo->node_ents there, before walking the entries.

t: xfs: bound inode fork length against the fork size during log recovery
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: bound inode fork length against the fork size during log recovery xlog_recover_inode_commit_pass2() copies an inode log item's data/attr fork region into the inode buffer using the on-log region length without bounding it against the fork capacity, e.g.: len = item->ri_buf[2].iov_len; memcpy(XFS_DFORK_DPTR(dip), src, len); The only guard is an ASSERT, which is a no-op on production kernels (CONFIG_XFS_DEBUG off), and xfs_dinode_verify() runs only after the copy. A crafted image with a dirty log can therefore drive a heap out-of-bounds write at mount time. The XFS_ILOG_DBROOT sibling already passes XFS_DFORK_DSIZE as a bound; the DDATA/DEXT and ADATA/AEXT memcpy paths did not. Bound each logged fork region against the destination fork size before copying it, and reject the log item with -EFSCORRUPTED when it does not fit. Because the recovered inode is only verified after the fork data has been copied in, the checks are done up front, before any memcpy into the on-disk inode.

t: xfs: complain loudly when dirtree checker finds broken links
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: complain loudly when dirtree checker finds broken links LOLLM observed that the directory tree walk code bails out if it finds broken parent pointers along the way. However, it flattens the return code to zero, which means that we can end up in the repair code having not completed the scan. We should never proceed with a repair in this state, so let's mark the scrub incomplete and exit.

t: xfs: don't overrun incore inode when cleaning attr forks
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: don't overrun incore inode when cleaning attr forks LOLLM noticed that xrep_dinode_check_afork doesn't check for a di_forkoff value that is so large that the attr fork would begin after the end of the inode space. This causes afork_{ptr,size} to be nonsense. What we really ought to do here is zap the attr fork.

t: xfs: don't subtract excess usage twice when computing agf_btreeblks
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: don't subtract excess usage twice when computing agf_btreeblks LOLLM noticed that the free space btree repair code calculates agf_btreeblks from the number of blocks we wrote to rebuild the free space btrees (minus the roots). That's correct. However, it observes that we subtract the "excess" reservation, which is not correct. Fix this accounting problem.

t: xfs: don't try to scrub self-referential dirent in metapath checker
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: don't try to scrub self-referential dirent in metapath checker LOLLM observes that the _ilock_both helper will loop forever trying to double-lock the same inode if mpath->dp == sc->ip. Callers are not supposed to call us with parent == child because that makes no sense. Trigger an assertion, mark the scan incomplete, and return IO error so that this fails noisily.

t: xfs: fix correction of unwritten extents in quota file data fork
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: xfs: fix correction of unwritten extents in quota file data fork LOLLM noticed a couple of problems with the code that fixes unwritten mappings in the quota file's data fork: first, we should zero the ondisk contents as part of converting them to "unwritten" just in case we crash shortly after the conversion. Second, and more importantly, it noticed that we fail to resynchronize the iext tree cursor after modifying the iext tree. If the tree shape changes, we could be in a world of hurt. Third, we should force a quotacheck if we reset an ondisk dquot. Fix all issues.

t: smb: server: size directory name conversion buffer correctly
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: smb: server: size directory name conversion buffer correctly A 2048-byte ASCII directory name needs 4098 bytes when converted to UTF-16, including the terminator. ksmbd_convert_dir_info_name() caps its allocation at PATH_MAX and writes past the end of that buffer. Allocate space for one UTF-16 code unit per input byte plus the terminator. Use kmalloc_array() to check the size calculation.

t: smb: smbdirect: fix buffer length underflow in RDMA transfers
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: smb: smbdirect: fix buffer length underflow in RDMA transfers When a remote buffer descriptor is larger than the remaining local buffer, smbdirect_connection_rdma_xmit() clamps its length and sets buf_len to zero. The common accounting code then subtracts the clamped length from buf_len, causing it to underflow. If another descriptor follows, the loop processes it with a wrapped remaining length and includes memory beyond the local buffer in the RDMA transfer. A client can trigger an out-of-bounds kernel write with an SMB WRITE request, or an out-of-bounds kernel read with an SMB READ request, by supplying multiple RDMA buffer descriptors with an oversized descriptor before the last one. Remove the premature assignment to buf_len. Subtracting the clamped length already consumes the remaining buffer, so the next iteration stops and only descriptors within the local buffer are used to build work requests.

t: smb: client: bound POSIX lock data area by response length
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: smb: client: bound POSIX lock data area by response length CIFSSMBPosixLock() receives a TRANS2 response whose server-provided DataOffset and DataCount are not required by validate_t2() to describe an interval inside the response. A server can therefore make the client read a cifs_posix_lock beyond the response buffer and return those kernel bytes through F_GETLK. Use smbCalcSize() to obtain the full response length after any multipart TRANS2 reassembly, then reject data areas that extend past it before dereferencing them.

t: smb: client: don't resurrect an exiting tcon from cached dir workers
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: smb: client: don't resurrect an exiting tcon from cached dir workers cfids_laundromat_worker() bumps tcon->tc_count for every expired open cfid and queues cached_dir_offload_close() without checking whether the tcon is already being torn down. Racing with the final cifs_put_tcon(), the tcon comes back from zero and gets torn down twice: T1 T2 cifs_put_tcon() --tc_count == 0, TID_EXITING tconInfoFree() free_cached_dirs() cancel_delayed_work_sync() cfids_laundromat_worker() ++tc_count == 1 queue_work(serverclose_wq) kfree(tcon->origin_fullpath) kfree(tcon) cached_dir_offload_close() close_cached_dir() [UAF] cifs_put_tcon() tconInfoFree() [double free] cached_dir_lease_break() also bumps tc_count without tc_lock, racing with the laundromat's locked update. Take the tcon reference through a helper that refuses once the tcon is TID_EXITING or its refcount has dropped to zero. Queued put_work and close_work then always hold a tcon reference, so tconInfoFree() can't run before they finish and free_cached_dirs() doesn't need to flush any workqueue. If the laundromat can't get a reference, put the cfid back on the dying list for free_cached_dirs() to free; its handle goes away with the tree connection. The lease break path finds the tcon on ses->tcon_list under cifs_tcp_ses_lock, so it can't see TID_EXITING, but it now takes tc_lock.

t: smb: client: fix buffer overflow in SMB2_tcon()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: smb: client: fix buffer overflow in SMB2_tcon() In SMB2_tcon(), unc_path is allocated with a fixed buffer size of MAX_SHARENAME_LENGTH * 2 bytes (672 bytes). However, the user-controlled UNC path (tree) length is passed to cifs_strtoUTF16(), which assumes the destination buffer is large enough and writes strlen(tree) + 1 UTF-16 code units. Commit 62a1a439e0fd ("cifs: clean up handling of unc= option") removed the length check on UNC mount options, allowing mount paths to exceed MAX_SHARENAME_LENGTH while retaining the fixed-size buffer allocation in SMB2_tcon(). Consequently, an oversized UNC string causes cifs_strtoUTF16() to write past the end of the heap object, resulting in a slab-out-of-bounds write. Furthermore, if a tree exceeds MAX_TREE_SIZE characters, strscpy() truncates it in cifs_tcon::tree_name, causing subsequent reconnects or failovers to fail. Fix this by first verifying that the length of tree does not exceed MAX_TREE_SIZE, returning -EINVAL if it does. Then, dynamically allocate unc_path based on the length of tree so that it safely accommodates all UTF-16 code units for paths within MAX_TREE_SIZE. [pc: remove unused MAX_SHARENAME_LENGTH]

t: smb: client: fix OOB read of the resume name sent in TRANS2_FIND_NEXT2
